idiom_name: refcounted intern pool over a hash table (g_ref_string_new_intern-style)
implementation_notes: C has no object model to share, so the classic roles are written by hand: an immutable struct holding only the intrinsic fields, a hash table keyed by them (hcreate/hsearch or a custom open-addressing table with strcmp keys), and an explicit reference count per entry so the canonical instance can be freed when its last handle is released. GLib ships exactly this shape: g_ref_string_new_intern() returns a new reference to an existing string instead of allocating a second copy, and the interned table entry is removed when the count reaches zero. Without a garbage collector, sharing must be paired with ref/unref discipline or with an arena that is freed as one unit; the shared struct is treated as const by convention only, since nothing in the type system enforces it.
pitfalls: There is no garbage collector: every handle taken from the pool must be released (refcount or arena reset) or the intern table becomes a leak that is invisible at the sharing site.
hsearch() maintains one process-global table that never shrinks and needs its capacity chosen up front; hcreate_r() is required for more than one pool.
The table key must be owned by the pool (copied) or guaranteed outlived by it - storing a caller's stack buffer as the key leaves dangling pointers.
The shared struct is const only by convention: one write through a cast-away handle corrupts every user of that glyph, and C's type system will not stop it.
